passage: At half past six, before the Oslo streets were light, Ingrid was already at the pool, swimming lengths while the lifeguard yawned. Her chemistry test was that afternoon, and she had revised till midnight. When the grades went up on the class screen, she scanned for her name before anything else. Second. Clara, beside her, whooped at her own B. 'Ingrid, you got an A-minus! Why do you look like someone died?' 'Jonas got an A.' 'So?' Ingrid didn't answer. Mr Halvorsen had written 'Good, but careless in question four' under her mark, and she read it five times. That evening Clara texted about a film. Ingrid replied, 'Can't. Redoing question four.' She fell asleep over the textbook with the light still on.

qa.q: What did Mr Halvorsen write under Ingrid's mark?
qa.a: 'Good, but careless in question four.'

qa.q: Why did Ingrid look so gloomy about an A-minus?
qa.a: Ingrid felt disappointed and anxious because she measured herself by coming first and by her teacher's praise, so second place felt like failing.

qa.a: She could set a fixed stopping time for study and say yes to the film sometimes, treating rest as part of the work rather than a waste.

qa.a: Clara is puzzled and a bit worried; to her an A-minus is great news, so Ingrid's gloom seems out of proportion.

passage: The rank list went up outside the hostel mess on Friday evening, and Disha pushed through the crowd to read it. First in the mock test, again. At dinner the principal stopped by her table. 'Our topper,' he said, and patted her shoulder. Disha felt that pat for an hour, warm as sunlight. Then Rekha, her roommate, came in with glitter on her cheeks. 'Talent night starts at eight. You're coming, na? Just one song.' 'Next test is in nine days.' 'Disha, you're first!' 'That's why.' She went back to the room and opened her physics book. Down the corridor, music started. She read the same line again and again. What if next time the principal walked past her table? She stayed up until two, and could not say if she had learned anything.

qa.q: Where did the rank list go up?
qa.a: Outside the hostel mess on Friday evening.

qa.q: What was Disha worried about as the music started?
qa.a: Disha was anxious about losing first place and the principal's praise, so even success felt fragile and left no room to relax.

qa.a: They could praise her effort and kindness as well as her rank, and nudge her towards events like talent night, so her worth isn't tied to one list.

qa.a: Rekha may feel shut out and puzzled, since she wanted to share a fun evening and her roommate's success seems to make things tenser, not lighter.

passage: I'm Rukmini, and last semester I became class representative for the second-year commerce batch. I'll admit I wanted it for the seat at the faculty table as much as anything else. The first month went well; I got a timetable clash fixed and people started saying, 'Ask Rukmini.' I liked that more than I expected. Then Pankaj suggested we vote on the date for the industrial visit. I said no, I'd already fixed it with the professor, it would save time. Pankaj said quietly, 'You didn't ask anyone.' I brushed it off. Later I heard three people couldn't go because of their part-time jobs. Looking back, it wasn't about saving time. I liked deciding. Now I put every big decision to a quick class poll, even when it's slower and I disagree with the result.

Mahima volunteered to lead her group of twelve for the campus clean-up and did it well: she split the tasks fairly, checked on the slowest team and thanked each person by name. At the wrap-up she told me she plans to stand for the students' council next year. 'I want to be the one they come to,' she said. Later, though, I watched her take the clipboard from Akash, who had been assigned sign-in, and redo his list without asking him. Akash went silent for the rest of the afternoon. I spoke to Mahima privately afterwards, praising her organising and asking how Akash might have felt. She paused, then went to return the clipboard. I'll check in with both of them next week.

Tuesday, a week before Pongal: Anand carried a new clay pot home to his Hyderabad flat, wrapped in newspaper like something alive. His flatmate Suraj laughed. 'You know you can just order sweet pongal, right?' 'It's not about the pongal,' Anand said, and didn't explain.
Pongal morning: he was up at five, drawing a crooked kolam at the door the way Paati did, then boiling milk in the clay pot on the gas. When it frothed over, he said 'Pongalo pongal!' to the kitchen, and felt his throat tighten. Suraj shuffled out, sleepy, and stood watching.
The next Sunday: Anand called Paati and described every detail. She laughed at the crooked kolam. Suraj, passing, leaned towards the phone. 'Paati, next year teach me the words too.'

qa.q: What did Anand draw at the door on Pongal morning?
qa.a: A crooked kolam, the way Paati did.

qa.a: Anand felt moved and a little homesick, his throat tightening as the old ritual connected him to Paati and home.

qa.a: He could invite Suraj and other friends from the start and share why the ritual matters, instead of not explaining.

qa.a: Suraj first treats it as a joke about ordering food, but after watching the morning asks Paati to teach the words too.

I also asked the warden to let me eat sehri early in the pantry, and the warden agreed. My roommate Grace started waking at four with me just to keep me company, though she wasn't fasting. I kept the fast, but I dropped some old ideas my aunts had, like girls not studying late. Both felt right.

Gurleen, from the batch of three years ago, came in to return a book and stayed to talk. I told her both feelings made sense and that a steady choice can still leave room for creative work. I gave her details of the college's evening design workshops, and she took the leaflet.

passage: In the Chennai flat, Gopika laid three sticky notes on the dining table: FREEDOM, SAFETY, FAMILY WAYS. The Bengaluru offer expired on Friday. Amma wanted her home until marriage, as the women of the family always had stayed. Her salary said she could manage alone. The job itself thrilled her. She moved the notes around for an hour. Then she put FREEDOM on top, but only for this decision. 'For the wedding, family ways can win,' she told herself. 'For my work, this time, I choose.' Her cousin Uma had stayed home and taken the local bank job last year. Gopika had privately thought it timid. Now she texted: 'Tell me how you decided. I'm deciding differently, but I want to understand.' Uma replied with a long voice note, and Gopika listened to all of it.

passage: Last winter I nearly resigned. I'm Mridul, and I've been a clerk in the municipal office for three years: fixed hours, a pension, my parents proud at every family wedding. Then Vinita, my friend from college, asked me to join her school project in the hills. Freedom, adventure, work that mattered. I lay awake making lists. What I finally saw was that I couldn't make freedom, security and my family's expectations all come first. For this one choice, security had to lead: my younger brother still had two years of college, and our father's health was shaky. I told Vinita no, and offered two weekends a month to help her train teachers. She said, 'I'd never choose your way.' I said, 'I know. I don't think you're wrong.' We still argue about it, happily, over the phone.

passage: Aparna, you're counting who gave you what on your birthday, so let me tell you about me at eight. It was Lohri, and Balwinder had the best kite in the village, red with a long tail. I had two sugarcane sticks and nothing else. 'I'll give you one stick if you give me the kite for ten minutes,' I said. Fair, na? He agreed. I flew it for exactly ten minutes by the gurdwara clock and handed it back, very proud of my honesty. Later that night his little sister cried because her kite string had snapped. I had a whole spool at home. Did I think of giving her some? No. She had nothing to trade. That's how I thought then, beta. For Santosh at eight, fair meant a deal.

qa.a: One sugarcane stick for ten minutes with the kite.

passage: Fog had made the school bus forty minutes late, and the half-yearly maths test was starting in five minutes. Nirmala slid into the seat next to Samir, breathless, and pressed her pencil to the paper. The tip snapped. 'Samir, sharpener? Please, quick!' Samir had a sharpener, a new blue one. He also had no eraser, and Nirmala had two. 'I'll lend my sharpener if you lend me one eraser for the whole test,' he whispered. 'That's fair.' 'Just give it, the teacher's coming!' 'Deal first.' Nirmala shoved an eraser at him, and he handed over the sharpener. Both started writing. Samir felt pleased with himself. It had been an even swap. passage:
Day one of the Ganesh festival holidays: Lavanya lent Aadhya her best thing, a wind-up train that whistled. 'Keep it till Sunday,' she said, feeling generous and grown-up.
Thursday: the colony pandal was lit up, and Aadhya was riding her new cycle round and round it. 'Can I have one turn?' Lavanya asked. 'No, it's new. Papa said.' Lavanya stood by the pandal steps, the drums loud, her face hot. She had given the train. For four whole days.
Sunday: Aadhya returned the train, one wheel wobbly, and said nothing about it. Lavanya put it on the top shelf. 'Never again,' she told her mother. 'I gave, she didn't give back. That's cheating.' Her mother began to answer, then just stroked her hair.

subtopic: Kohlberg self-interest stage
subtype: Feels cheated when kindness is not returned [Receiver]
passage: Pema, you're sulking because your friend didn't share back, so here's a story from when your Disha Aunty was nine. It was the week before Diwali in Siliguri, and I had a box of sparkly bindis from my mausi in Kolkata. My best friend Moni had nothing new for the festival, so I lent her half. I felt like a queen. Then, on Diwali night, Moni got a big box of sparklers and lit them with her cousins, and she never once called me over. I stood at our gate watching the lights across the lane. The next morning I marched over and took back every bindi. 'Never again,' I told her. 'You're a cheat.' It took us three weeks to talk again, and I still remember how my chest felt that night.

qa.q: What did Disha lend Moni before Diwali?
qa.a: Half the box of sparkly bindis.

qa.q: What did Disha feel standing at the gate on Diwali night?
qa.a: She felt hurt, left out and cheated, because she had shared and got nothing back; she still remembers how her chest felt.

qa.q: Disha marched over and took back every bindi. What else could she have done?
qa.a: She could have told Moni how hurt she felt watching from the gate, which might have led to an apology instead of three weeks of silence.

qa.q: How might Moni have seen the bindi incident?
qa.a: Moni may not have known Disha expected an invitation, so being called a cheat probably felt sudden and hurtful.

grounding: An aunt recalls being nine and feeling cheated when a friend she had shared with did not share back at Diwali.

subtopic: Kohlberg self-interest stage
subtype: Feels cheated when kindness is not returned [Receiver]
passage: The monsoon had been pouring for a week in Kochi. On Monday Joseph lent Anjali his big black umbrella because hers had snapped, and he walked home under a plastic bag, soaked to the socks. On Wednesday, with only ten minutes of lunch break left, Joseph's tiffin slipped off the wet bench and his idlis landed in a puddle. He looked straight at Anjali, who had a full box of lemon rice. She was busy copying homework and didn't look up. Joseph's stomach growled. He waited. Nothing. The bell rang. On the way back to class he muttered, 'I gave you my umbrella. I got wet for you. Never again.' Anjali blinked. 'What? I didn't even see.' Joseph didn't answer. He was too hungry to explain.

qa.q: What happened to Joseph's idlis?
qa.a: His tiffin slipped off the wet bench and his idlis landed in a puddle.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when Anjali didn't look up?
qa.a: Joseph felt hurt and cheated, since he had got soaked lending the umbrella and expected help in return.

qa.q: What could Joseph try instead of muttering 'never again'?
qa.a: He could simply ask Anjali to share, since she hadn't even seen what happened; asking clearly gives her the chance to help.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel on hearing 'Never again'?
qa.a: Anjali is likely confused and a little hurt, since she didn't notice the fallen tiffin and didn't know she had let Joseph down.

grounding: In a rainy week a boy who lent his umbrella feels wronged when the favour is not returned at lunch.

subtopic: Kohlberg self-interest stage
subtype: Helping a child see beyond the deal [Response]
passage: Karthik, you asked how I handled the swap-crazy kids in my Class 4. Let me tell you about Bilal. It was Christmas fair week, and the children were making paper stars to sell. Bilal would give glue only for glitter, glitter only for scissors, every deal exact. Then little Asha, whose father was in hospital, came with nothing. Bilal said, 'Pay me a sticker and you can use my glue.' She had no stickers. I didn't scold him. Children like fairness; it's a good start. I just crouched beside him and asked, 'Bilal, how would you feel if nobody shared with you, right when your papa was sick?' He looked at Asha for a long moment. Then he pushed the glue across. 'Harsha Ma'am, is that allowed?' I told him it was the kindest thing on that table all week.

qa.q: What did Bilal ask Asha to pay for using his glue?
qa.a: A sticker.

qa.q: What might Bilal have felt looking at Asha for a long moment?
qa.a: Bilal probably felt a pang of sympathy, imagining how lonely it would be if nobody shared while his papa was sick.

qa.q: Harsha chose to crouch beside Bilal and ask a question instead of scolding. Why was that a good turning point?
qa.a: It respected Bilal's instinct for fairness while turning his attention to Asha's feelings, so he chose to share on his own.

qa.q: How might Asha have felt when the glue was pushed across to her?
qa.a: Asha, already worried about her father, probably felt relieved and cared for, included without having to pay.

grounding: A retired teacher recalls using one question at a festival fair to move a trading child towards another child's feelings.

subtopic: Kohlberg self-interest stage

passage: Rain had cancelled the camp's outdoor games, and twenty children were crammed into the community hall with three board games between them. Omkar sat guarding the snakes-and-ladders board. 'Dev can play if he gives me his chips,' he announced. 'That's the deal.' Dev, whose lunchbox held only two rotis, looked at the floor. Rehana, the camp teacher, had ten minutes before parents arrived and a leak dripping into a bucket behind her. She knelt beside Omkar anyway. 'You like things fair, don't you?' 'Yes. He plays, I get something.' 'How would you feel if you had no chips and nobody let you play?' Omkar stared at Dev's lunchbox, then at the rain on the window. 'Bad,' he mumbled. He moved over. 'You can be red. It's the lucky one.'

qa.a: It suggests Omkar was starting to feel sorry for Dev, imagining being left out with nothing to trade.

qa.a: It was short, didn't shame Omkar's sense of fairness, and turned his attention to Dev's feelings, so he chose to include Dev himself.

qa.a: Dev goes from looking at the floor, embarrassed to have nothing to give, to being welcomed with the lucky red counter.

passage: In the village of Khedi, the mango orchard needed guarding every afternoon in May, and Jagdish knew it. At dinner he laid out his offer like a shopkeeper. subtopic: Kohlberg self-interest stage
passage: I'm Gurleen, and for my first two years at the logistics firm I kept a ledger in my head. Jagdish from accounts once asked me to cover his Saturday shift. I did it, and noted: he owes me one. When my laptop crashed before a big presentation, I cashed it in; he stayed late fixing my slides. Fair. I realised I had a lot of fair deals at that office and not one friend. I'm still working out what to do with that.

passage:
Wednesday night.
I opened my notes to add today's entry to the list: 'Nirmala: brought soup when I was down with flu. I owe her one.' Then I scrolled up. Three years of entries. Who covered whose shift, who introduced whom to which client, who remembered my birthday so I remembered theirs. Everything balanced. Tidy. Fair. But Nirmala didn't bring the soup to collect anything. She just sat on my sofa, asked about Amma, and left. I tried to offer her my weekend shift as payback and she looked hurt. 'It was soup, Sangeeta, not a loan.' I've been sitting here an hour. I can't remember the last time I helped someone at work just because they looked tired. I don't think the list has ever made anyone sit on my sofa.

qa.a: Sangeeta feels unsettled and a little lonely, noticing that all the fair accounts have left no one who simply cares.

qa.a: Sangeeta could offer help without writing it down or expecting anything back, and see how the relationship changes.
